content.overview: Public Interest Litigation relaxes traditional locus standi so that a person acting bona fide may move the court to enforce constitutional or legal rights of persons who cannot approach the court themselves, or to compel performance of public duties. PIL is a rule of standing and access; it does not create a new substantive writ or convert every social grievance into a justiciable claim.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Is the petitioner acting bona fide in public interest? (2) Whose rights or public duty is engaged? (3) Why can the directly affected class not approach the court effectively? (4) Is the chosen forum Article 32 or 226? (5) Is the petition a private dispute or rivalry dressed as PIL?
content.study:
Core rule: ordinary civil and constitutional practice required the petitioner to show personal injury or a direct legal interest. PIL liberalises that rule for genuine public-interest claims so that disadvantaged persons and diffuse public duties can reach the court.

What liberalised standing is: A bona fide petitioner may sue not only for personal rights but for the rights of others who cannot approach the court, or to enforce a public duty owed to the community. Standing is therefore about who may be heard, not about inventing a new cause of action.

What it is not: PIL is not a licence for private disputes, contractual rivalries, service grievances, or personal vendettas. Those fail the bona fide public-interest test and are controlled under abuse-of-process and costs principles.

Forum link: Liberalised standing operates through the existing writ jurisdictions — Article 32 in the Supreme Court for fundamental rights, and Article 226 in the High Courts for fundamental rights and other legal rights. Choice of forum still depends on the nature of the right and the appropriate territorial and subject-matter reach.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in Articles 32 and 226 and in the bona fide public-interest test. Do not treat evidence statutes as the source of standing doctrine. Case names used for orientation in this topic remain subject to separate authoritative verification; no holding is treated as verified solely because it appears in study text.

sections.heading: Traditional locus standi and the PIL departure
sections.body: Traditional practice required the petitioner to be a person aggrieved — someone whose legal right was personally invaded. PIL relaxes that requirement for bona fide public-interest petitions so that persons unable to approach the court, and duties owed to the public, are not left without a remedy merely because of poverty, ignorance, or fear.

sections.heading: Who may approach and on what basis
sections.body: A petitioner may be heard if they act bona fide in the public interest, identify the right or public duty engaged, and show why the class directly affected cannot effectively approach the court themselves. Good faith and public purpose are essential; the petition must not be a private dispute in disguise.

sections.heading: Link to Articles 32 and 226
sections.body: Liberalised standing does not create a new writ. Relief is still sought under Article 32 (Supreme Court — fundamental rights) or Article 226 (High Courts — fundamental rights and other legal rights). The standing rule opens the door; the constitutional provision supplies the jurisdiction and the available remedies.

sections.heading: Abuse filters and the limits of liberal standing
sections.body: Courts filter petitions that are motivated by personal rivalry, publicity, or private commercial interest. Where the petition fails the bona fide public-interest test, it may be dismissed and costs may follow. Liberal standing is therefore paired with responsibility — see the companion topic on limits and costs.

sections.heading: Analytical steps for a standing challenge
sections.body: (1) Identify the right or public duty. (2) Identify the class affected and why they cannot approach. (3) Test the petitioner's bona fides. (4) Choose the correct forum (32 or 226). (5) Separate standing from the merits of the substantive claim.

provisions.title: Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for fundamental rights
High Court writ jurisdiction for fundamental rights and other legal rights

examples.title: Disadvantaged class cannot approach
examples.body: A social worker moves the High Court under Article 226 complaining of bonded labour in a district, acting for workers who are illiterate and economically dependent on the employers. The issue is whether liberalised standing is available for a bona fide public-interest claim on behalf of persons who cannot approach the court effectively.

examples.title: Private dispute dressed as PIL
examples.body: A contractor who lost a tender files a 'PIL' alleging corruption in the award process, seeking cancellation of the successful bid. The issue is whether the petition is a private commercial grievance rather than a bona fide public-interest claim, and whether standing should be denied under the abuse filter.

examples.title: Forum choice after standing is accepted
examples.body: A bona fide petitioner challenges a state action as violating a fundamental right of a vulnerable group. Standing is not disputed. The remaining issue is whether the petition belongs under Article 32 or Article 226 given the right engaged and the appropriate court.

hypotheticals.question: Does every citizen have an automatic right to file a PIL on any public issue?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Liberalised standing requires bona fide public interest, a justiciable right or public duty, and usually a reason why the directly affected class cannot approach. Private disputes and motivated petitions fail the test.

hypotheticals.question: If standing is accepted, does that decide the merits?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Standing decides who may be heard. The court still examines maintainability, alternative remedies where relevant, and the substantive constitutional or legal claim on its own terms.

distinctions.title: Traditional locus standi vs PIL liberalised standing
distinctions.left: Traditional standing: petitioner must show personal legal injury or direct interest.
distinctions.right: PIL standing: bona fide petitioner may sue for others who cannot approach or to enforce a public duty.

rows.left: Person aggrieved in the private-law sense.
rows.right: Bona fide public-interest representative or concerned citizen where criteria are met.
Rights of disadvantaged classes; enforcement of public duties.

distinctions.title: Standing vs cause of action
distinctions.left: Standing: who is entitled to be heard.
distinctions.right: Cause of action: whether a legal claim on the merits exists.

rows.left: May this petitioner move the court?
rows.right: Has a constitutional or legal right been violated or a public duty breached?

rows.left: Petition not maintainable for want of standing.
rows.right: Petition may fail on merits even if standing is accepted.

misconceptions.trap: PIL creates a new kind of writ independent of Articles 32 and 226.
misconceptions.correction: PIL is a rule of standing and access. Relief is still sought under the existing constitutional writ jurisdictions.

misconceptions.trap: Any public-spirited person can litigate any policy disagreement as PIL.
misconceptions.correction: The petition must be bona fide, justiciable, and not a private dispute or motivated rivalry; abuse filters and costs apply.

misconceptions.trap: Acceptance of standing means the petitioner has won the case.
misconceptions.correction: Standing only opens the door. Merits, maintainability and appropriate relief remain separate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a PIL standing objection be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. State the traditional person-aggrieved rule. II. State the PIL liberalisation for bona fide public-interest claims. III. Identify the right or public duty and the class affected. IV. Test the petitioner's bona fides and exclude private disputes. V. Link standing to Article 32 or 226. VI. Separate standing from merits and relief.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain the concept of locus standi in Public Interest Litigation. How does it differ from traditional standing?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Introduce traditional person-aggrieved standing. Explain PIL liberalisation for bona fide public-interest claims on behalf of those who cannot approach the court or to enforce public duties. Stress that PIL is a standing rule, not a new writ. Link to Articles 32 and 226. Note abuse filters. Conclude with the distinction between standing and merits.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Discuss liberalised locus standi in PIL. Examine its justification, limits, and relationship with Articles 32 and 226.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Traditional standing and access barriers. II. Justification for liberalisation (disadvantaged classes; public duties). III. Criteria: bona fides, public interest, justiciable claim. IV. Forum: Articles 32 and 226. V. Limits: private disputes, rivalry, costs. VI. Standing vs cause of action. VII. Conclusion: liberal access with responsibility.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on PIL standing contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the right or public duty; explain why the affected class cannot approach; demonstrate the petitioner's bona fides; answer the objection that the dispute is private or motivated; state the correct forum under Article 32 or 226; and keep standing arguments separate from the merits prayer.

examTips: Open by contrasting traditional person-aggrieved standing with PIL liberalisation.
Always test bona fides and exclude private disputes.
Name Article 32 or 226 as the jurisdictional vehicle.
Do not invent case holdings; use only verified authorities when the verification gate is complete.
